Family Health

Ovarian cysts and lower back pain: is there a connection?

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Many ovarian cysts cause no symptoms and disappear without treatment. Some, especially larger cysts, can cause pelvic pressure or a dull lower-back ache. Back pain alone cannot identify a cyst, and finding a cyst on a scan does not prove it explains the pain. Assessment should consider both pelvic and spinal causes.

How a cyst may be linked to back pain

An ovarian cyst is a fluid-filled sac in or on an ovary. Functional cysts develop around ovulation and are common before menopause. Larger cysts may put pressure on nearby structures and cause lower-abdominal or pelvic discomfort that can be felt in the lower back or thighs. The ache may come and go; not everyone with a large cyst has pain.

The source article refers to a selected imaging series. Such figures cannot establish how often ovarian cysts cause back pain in the general population, or whether an incidental cyst caused an individual’s symptoms. Muscle strain, disc or nerve problems and other pelvic, urinary or bowel conditions can produce similar pain.

Symptoms do not confirm the cause

Possible accompanying symptoms include pelvic fullness, bloating, painful or irregular periods, unusual vaginal bleeding, pain during sex, urinary frequency or difficulty emptying the bladder, and constipation or bowel pressure. Burning urination also needs assessment for other causes, including infection. These symptoms are not specific to cysts.

New leg weakness, tingling or numbness should not be attributed to a cyst without assessment. Back pain with new numbness around the genitals or anus, weakness or numbness in both legs, or new difficulty urinating or loss of bladder or bowel control needs immediate emergency care. Do not wait for a planned ovarian scan.

Different types of ovarian cyst

Functional cysts include follicular cysts, when a follicle does not release its egg as expected, and corpus luteum cysts, when fluid collects after ovulation. Many resolve over weeks or a few cycles. A normal developing follicle is not automatically a harmful cyst, and not every ovarian cyst has the same size or course.

Dermoid cysts, also called mature cystic teratomas, arise from germ cells and may contain fat, skin, hair or teeth. They are usually benign but need an individual assessment. Cystadenomas develop from ovarian surface tissue, may contain watery fluid or mucus, and can grow large.

Endometriomas contain old blood and are associated with endometriosis. Endometriosis itself can cause pelvic, period-related or back pain. Cyst type, appearance, growth, symptoms and age matter together; size alone neither diagnoses the cause of pain nor determines whether surgery is necessary.

How clinicians investigate the pain

A clinician asks about where and when pain occurs, its relation to periods or movement, bleeding, urinary or bowel symptoms, medicines and pregnancy possibility. Examination may include the abdomen, back and, with consent when appropriate, the pelvis. A pregnancy test can be important even when a cyst is already known.

Pelvic ultrasound assesses a cyst’s location, size and whether it looks simple, solid or complex. Abdominal or vaginal ultrasound is selected according to the situation and your consent. A scan can identify a cyst but cannot by itself establish that it causes back pain; other investigations may be needed.

Blood tests, including CA-125, are selected rather than required for every simple cyst. CA-125 may rise in cancer but also in noncancerous conditions such as endometriosis or pelvic inflammation. Menopausal status, scan findings and the whole clinical picture guide interpretation; a result alone is not a diagnosis.

Comfort measures while following a care plan

If symptoms are mild and a clinician has advised observation, wrapped warmth may ease discomfort. Avoid burns. Gentle activity or stretching can help some back pain, but stop if pain worsens and do not try to exercise through severe pelvic pain. Prolonged bed rest is usually unhelpful for ordinary back pain. These measures do not shrink or cure a cyst.

A clinician or pharmacist can help select pain relief. Paracetamol/acetaminophen may be considered for pelvic discomfort; it is not generally recommended alone for nonspecific back pain. Ibuprofen or naproxen may be unsuitable with pregnancy, kidney disease, previous stomach ulcers, bleeding risk or certain medicines. Do not combine NSAIDs or take them in pregnancy without professional advice; follow the product instructions.

When to arrange assessment

Seek assessment for persistent, recurrent, worsening or disabling pain, new pelvic symptoms, unexplained weight loss or pain that is worse at night. Fever or feeling generally unwell with back or pelvic pain needs urgent advice. New pain after injury, unusual bleeding or changes in bladder or bowel function should be discussed rather than assumed to be a familiar cyst.

If pregnancy is possible, pelvic pain or unusual vaginal bleeding needs prompt medical advice, even without a positive pregnancy test. Ectopic pregnancy is one possible cause. Shoulder-tip pain needs advice immediately; sudden severe abdominal pain with dizziness or fainting needs emergency care.

Monitoring and hormonal medicines

Observation may be suitable for a cyst that appears benign, depending on symptoms, age, pregnancy or menopausal status, size and scan features. Some need a repeat scan and others do not. Agree on the follow-up date and what changes should prompt an earlier review; do not apply one interval to every cyst.

A December 2025 RCOG update states that an asymptomatic, simple, unilateral, unilocular cyst measuring 3 cm or less after menopause does not need routine follow-up. This specific low-risk finding does not apply to every postmenopausal cyst or to unexplained symptoms. Local guidance and individual circumstances still matter.

Hormonal contraception that suppresses ovulation may reduce new functional cysts in suitable people, but it does not shrink an existing cyst or treat every cyst type. Discuss contraceptive preferences, pregnancy plans, risks and alternatives; do not start hormones solely on the basis of back pain.

When surgery may be appropriate

Surgery may be considered for a cyst that is growing, persistent, large, concerning on imaging or causing significant symptoms. Cancer concern, torsion or bleeding changes the urgency and plan. Persistence beyond a few cycles does not automatically mean every cyst needs removal.

Keyhole surgery (laparoscopy) is often possible for suitable benign-looking cysts; an open operation may be needed for a very large cyst or suspected cancer. Cystectomy removes the cyst while retaining ovarian tissue when possible; oophorectomy removes an ovary when necessary. Discuss fertility, ovarian preservation and the possibility of a different operation beforehand. Removing a cyst cannot guarantee relief if back pain has another cause.

Rupture, bleeding and twisting of the ovary

A ruptured cyst can cause sudden pain and sometimes internal bleeding. Some people can be observed with pain relief after assessment, while significant bleeding or instability may need hospital monitoring, intravenous fluids, transfusion or surgery. Rupture is not always harmless or always treated with an operation.

Torsion means the ovary twists and its blood supply is threatened. It needs urgent gynaecological assessment and may require prompt surgery to untwist and preserve the ovary. It can occur without a large cyst, especially in younger people. Ultrasound blood flow alone cannot reliably exclude torsion; severe symptoms should not be dismissed because of one reassuring finding.

Emergency signs: act on symptoms

Get immediate medical help for sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain, especially with nausea or vomiting, or pain with fever and marked illness. Fainting, major weakness, cold clammy skin or rapid breathing can signal serious bleeding or shock. Seek emergency care for severe pain with these signs rather than waiting for home treatment to work.

Back pain with new saddle-area numbness, symptoms in both legs, new urinary retention or loss of bladder or bowel control requires immediate emergency assessment for a spinal problem. A serious accident or chest pain with back pain also needs emergency care. A known ovarian cyst does not rule out another emergency.

Following up without assuming every pain is the cyst

Many functional cysts resolve and many other cysts remain benign, but the plan should fit the actual findings. Keep the agreed appointments and ask which symptoms require urgent contact. If pain continues despite cyst improvement or treatment, reassess other causes rather than repeating an assumption.

Record pain location and severity, its timing with periods or movement, bleeding, urinary or bowel changes, medicines and scan dates. Bring pregnancy or fertility concerns to the discussion. Monitoring symptoms can support a consultation, but cannot diagnose a cyst, cancer, torsion or a spinal emergency.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Current Cleveland Clinic and Mayo Clinic information recognizes possible back ache while emphasizing variable symptoms, cyst type and individual treatment.

March 2026 NHS back-pain advice distinguishes ordinary self-care from spinal warning signs needing emergency assessment.

The December 2025 RCOG postmenopausal update limits no-follow-up advice to a specific asymptomatic simple cyst finding; it is not a rule for all cysts.

Hormonal contraception may prevent new functional cysts but does not shrink existing cysts; rupture and torsion require assessment according to severity.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record pain patterns, period timing, bleeding, urinary or bowel changes, medicines and follow-up questions. Notes cannot prove that a cyst causes pain, interpret a scan or rule out cancer, torsion, ectopic pregnancy or a spinal emergency.

When to seek help

Seek immediate help for sudden severe pelvic pain, particularly with vomiting, fever or marked illness, or fainting, cold clammy skin, weakness or rapid breathing. New saddle numbness, symptoms in both legs, urinary retention or loss of bladder/bowel control needs emergency assessment. If pregnancy is possible, get prompt advice for pelvic pain or unusual bleeding. Do not delay care for a scan or home remedy.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A cyst can sometimes cause lower-back ache, but back pain or an incidental scan finding does not prove the connection.
  • Functional, dermoid, cystadenoma and endometrioma cysts have different courses and treatment needs.
  • Ultrasound findings, symptoms, age and pregnancy or menopausal status guide care; CA-125 alone is not a diagnosis.
  • Observation, suitable pain relief, hormonal prevention of new functional cysts or selected surgery require an individual plan.
  • Sudden severe pelvic pain, shock signs or new spinal nerve/bladder/bowel symptoms need immediate assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Can an ovarian cyst cause back pain?

Yes, some cysts, especially larger ones, can cause a dull ache in the lower back or thighs. Many cause no symptoms. Back pain has many other causes, so assessment is needed rather than assuming a cyst is responsible.

Which other symptoms may occur?

Pelvic fullness, bloating, period changes, unusual bleeding, pain during sex, urinary frequency or bowel pressure may occur. None is specific to a cyst. New leg weakness, saddle numbness or bladder/bowel control changes require urgent assessment, with emergency care for the warning combinations described above.

What cyst types can be associated with pain?

Functional cysts, dermoids, cystadenomas and endometriomas can sometimes cause pain. Many functional cysts disappear; endometriosis may cause pain even apart from an endometrioma. Type and size alone cannot identify the source of every backache.

What are dermoid cysts?

They are usually benign germ-cell growths, also called mature cystic teratomas, which may contain fat, skin, hair or teeth. Their assessment and treatment depend on symptoms and other findings; they are not the same as an ovulation-related functional cyst.

Will the contraceptive pill shrink a cyst?

No. Ovulation-suppressing hormonal contraception may help prevent new functional cysts in suitable people, but does not shrink an existing cyst or treat every type. Discuss risks and pregnancy plans before choosing it.

Does every cyst need repeat scans or surgery?

No. Follow-up depends on symptoms and scan features as well as age and pregnancy or menopausal status. Some low-risk cysts need no routine follow-up; selected growing, concerning or symptomatic cysts may need surgery.

Is a ruptured cyst always harmless?

No. Some are managed with observation and pain relief after assessment, but internal bleeding can be serious. Sudden severe pain, fainting, weakness, clammy skin or rapid breathing needs immediate help.

When is back pain an emergency?

New numbness around the genitals or anus, symptoms in both legs, urinary retention or loss of bladder or bowel control needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not assume these symptoms are caused by a known cyst.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
